questions.q: What does a Date object store?
questions.explain: A Date is an instant. Every zone-related method has to choose a zone at the moment you call it, which is where the bugs come from.
options: A year, month, day, hour, minute and second in the machine's time zone
One number: milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, with no time zone
A timestamp plus the time zone it was created in

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Months in Date.UTC and the Date constructor start at 0, so 3 is April. It is the most common date bug in JavaScript.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Subtracting dates subtracts their timestamps in milliseconds; dividing by 60,000 gives minutes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The string is not a format JavaScript understands, so the Date is invalid (timestamp NaN). Creating it does not throw, and JSON.stringify writes null silently. toISOString would throw.
questions.code:
const d = new Date("31/12/2026");
console.log(Number.isNaN(d.getTime()), JSON.stringify({ due: d }));

questions.q: A server computes order.placedAt.getDate() to print "ordered on the 4th". Why is this fragile?
questions.explain: Local getters depend on the machine. Use getUTCDate for UTC, or Intl.DateTimeFormat with an explicit timeZone for a particular place.
options: getDate returns the day of the week
getDate uses the time zone of the machine running the code, so the same order can print different days on servers in different regions

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: UTC getters read the instant in UTC: 3 March at 23:00, a Tuesday (getUTCDay counts Sunday as 0). They give the same answer on every machine.
questions.code:
const placedAt = new Date("2026-03-03T23:30:00Z");
console.log(placedAt.getUTCDate(), placedAt.getUTCHours(), placedAt.getUTCDay());

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Lagos is UTC+1 all year, so 23:30 UTC is 00:30 the next day in Lagos. Naming the zone makes the result independent of the machine.

questions.q: Why should a shop store timeZone: "Europe/London" rather than offset: "+00:00" for its London branch?
questions.explain: An offset describes one moment. A time zone describes which offset applies when, including daylight saving time.
options: Offsets are not supported in JavaScript
London's offset changes during the year (+00:00 in winter, +01:00 in summer); a zone name carries the rules, an offset is only true for part of the year

questions.q: British Summer Time starts on 29 March 2026. What does this print?
questions.explain: Adding 24 hours of milliseconds lands at 12:00 UTC on Sunday, which is 13:00 in London after the clocks went forward. "Same time tomorrow" is a calendar step, not a duration.

questions.q: Does the 23-hour-day problem affect a delivery schedule computed in Africa/Lagos?
questions.explain: West Africa Time has no DST. The bug appears as soon as the same code handles London, New York or any zone that changes its clocks.
options: No: Lagos stays at UTC+1 all year, but code that also serves zones with DST, or runs its calendar logic in such a zone, must still handle it
Yes, because UTC has daylight saving time

questions.q: How does new Date("2026-03-04") interpret the string?
questions.explain: Date-only ISO strings are UTC. Confusingly, a date-time without a zone ("2026-03-04T09:00") is read as local time.
options: As midnight in the machine's local time zone
As noon UTC, to avoid date shifts
It is invalid without a time

questions.q: A form sends "2026-03-04T09:00" for a delivery slot, and the server does new Date(slot). What is wrong?
questions.explain: The same code gives 09:00 UTC on a UTC server and 08:00 UTC on a Lagos server. Refuse zone-less date-times from clients.
options: Nothing; the string is valid ISO 8601
Without a zone the string is read as the server's local time, so the instant depends on where the server runs; the client must send an offset or a zone
The seconds are missing, so the result is invalid
It is always read as UTC, which is too late

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 09:00 at +01:00 is 08:00 UTC. toISOString always prints UTC with a Z.

questions.q: What does this print in Node.js or Chrome?
questions.explain: V8 accepts day 30 in February and rolls it over into March; month 13 is rejected. Other engines differ, so check parsed dates with a round trip.

questions.q: What does the lesson's strict parser do to reject "2026-02-30T00:00:00Z"?
questions.explain: Date.parse alone accepts it in V8. The round-trip check catches every impossible day, whichever engine you run on.
options: It compares the string with a list of valid dates
After parsing, it rebuilds the year, month and day with Date.UTC and checks they did not roll over into another month

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify uses toJSON, which returns the ISO string. JSON has no date type, so parsing gives back a string that you must convert yourself.

questions.q: How should an API store a customer's birthday?
questions.explain: A birthday is not an instant. Stored as midnight UTC and shown in a zone behind UTC, it becomes the previous day.
options: As a timestamp at midnight UTC
As a timestamp at midnight in the customer's zone
As a calendar date string, "1995-06-14" (a date column in the database)
As the number of days since 1970

questions.q: Which is the best JSON value for "the moment the payment succeeded"?
questions.explain: An ISO 8601 string in UTC with Z is unambiguous and sorts correctly as text. The others either lack a zone or are meant for people.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Working in UTC, every day is exactly 86,400,000 ms, so adding days is safe. 2026 is not a leap year; 2028 is.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "31 February" does not exist, so it rolls over three days into March. Day 0 of March rolls back to the last day of February, which is how you find a month's length.

questions.q: A subscription starts on 31 January and bills "monthly". Why does the billing code need an explicit rule?
questions.explain: Month arithmetic is a business decision. Clamping gives 28 February (29 in leap years), then 31 March.
options: Many months have no day 31; without a rule, JavaScript's rollover moves the date into the next month (3 March), so the business must choose, usually clamping to the month's last day
Because January has 31 days and February has 30
It does not; monthly billing is the same as every 30 days

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: reminder and config.launch are the same object, and set… methods change it in place. Copy with new Date(date) before adjusting.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: getUTCDay returns 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday). 1 October 2026 is a Thursday and 7 March 2026 a Saturday.

questions.q: The shop's rule says "orders before 14:00 Lagos time ship the same day". Which condition matches it?
questions.explain: "Before 14:00" excludes 14:00:00, so < 14. The hour must be read in the shop's zone: UTC is an hour behind Lagos, and local getters depend on the server.
options: hour < 14, where hour is the Lagos wall-clock hour of the order

questions.q: A delivery date is stored as "2026-03-06". How should it be formatted for display so the day can never shift?
questions.explain: A calendar date has no zone. Formatting midnight UTC in UTC always shows the same day; formatting it in a zone behind UTC shows the day before.
options: Parse it as local midnight and format in the customer's zone
Turn it into midnight UTC and format it with timeZone: "UTC"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: numeric: "auto" uses words like "yesterday" where the language has them. In English there is no single common word for −2 days, so it falls back to "2 days ago".
questions.code:
const rtf = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" });
console.log(rtf.format(-1, "day"), "|", rtf.format(1, "day"), "|", rtf.format(-2, "day"));
options: 1 day ago | in 1 day | 2 days ago
yesterday | tomorrow | the day before yesterday

questions.q: Why does the lesson's ago(then, now) take now as a parameter instead of calling Date.now() inside?
questions.explain: Reading the clock inside logic makes results depend on when the code runs. Pass the time in, or inject a clock function.
options: So the function is deterministic: tests pass fixed values and get the same output on every run
Because Date.now() does not exist in browsers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: formatToParts returns the pieces of the Lagos wall time. The month is a normal 1-based number here, and hourCycle: "h23" gives 0 for midnight rather than 24.

questions.q: An order is placed on Wednesday 30 September 2026 at 16:00 Lagos time. Processing starts the next business day, delivery is 2 business days later, and 1 October is a public holiday. What is the delivery date?
questions.explain: After the cut-off, processing moves to the next business day: Thursday is a holiday, so Friday 2 October. Two business days later, skipping the weekend: Monday 5, then Tuesday 6 October.

questions.q: Why does the estimator's test run the same cases with process.env.TZ set to several zones?
questions.explain: A test that only runs in the developer's zone can pass for months and fail on the first deployment elsewhere.
options: To test daylight saving time in Lagos
A hidden local getter or zone-less parse only fails when the machine's zone changes; running under several zones proves the result does not depend on where the code runs

questions.q: Which statement about the Temporal API is true at the time of the lesson?
questions.explain: Temporal fixes Date's design problems. Check availability in every runtime you deploy to before relying on it.
options: It is available in Node.js 24 and all browsers
It separates instants, zoned date-times, plain dates and durations, is immutable, and ships in Chromium but not in Node.js 24, where a polyfill is needed
It is a library you install from npm only

questions.q: In Temporal, what is Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-01-31").add({ months: 1 }) by default?
questions.explain: Temporal's default overflow behaviour is to constrain (clamp) to the last valid day, the rule you had to write by hand with Date.

questions.q: Two servers record events with Date.now(). Why should you not use those timestamps to decide which of two events happened first when they are milliseconds apart?
questions.explain: Clock drift and synchronisation adjustments make cross-machine timestamps unreliable at fine resolution.
options: The servers' clocks can disagree by more than that; use a single source of ordering such as a database sequence or the database's clock
Because timestamps are always in local time

questions.q: A test compares formatter.formatRange(a, b) with the string "30 Mar – 2 Apr 2026" typed in the test file. It passes in Chromium and fails in Node.js. Why?
questions.explain: Normalise whitespace (for example .replace(/\s/g, " ")) or compare formatToParts results when testing formatted text across runtimes.
options: Node.js formats dates in the server's zone
Intl output can contain special space characters (thin, no-break), and which ones depends on the locale data version; here Node uses thin spaces around the dash
The dash is a hyphen in Chromium

questions.q: Which of these should be computed by adding milliseconds to a timestamp?
questions.explain: A duration is a fixed amount of elapsed time, so milliseconds are right. Calendar steps and recurring wall times need calendar rules in a named zone.
options: "The same time tomorrow" for a London delivery slot
"The first day of next month" for an invoice

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend about the TZ setting of production servers?
questions.explain: UTC servers avoid surprises in logs and cron jobs, but correctness must come from explicit zones in the code, which the multi-zone tests verify.
options: Set it to the zone of most customers, such as Africa/Lagos
Run servers in UTC, and still write code that does not depend on the machine's zone
Leave it unset; Node.js ignores it
Change it per request to the customer's zone

questions.q: Write lagosDate(instant) that returns the calendar date in Lagos as "YYYY-MM-DD", using Intl.DateTimeFormat with timeZone: "Africa/Lagos" and formatToParts (no local getters).
questions.explain: Lagos is UTC+1, so the date changes at 23:00 UTC. 2-digit gives zero-padded months and days, ready for the string.

questions.q: Write addDays(date, days) for calendar-date strings "YYYY-MM-DD", doing the arithmetic in UTC, so it works on any machine.
questions.explain: In UTC every day is exactly 86,400,000 ms, so adding whole days never crosses a DST change. The Z makes the parse independent of the machine.

questions.q: Write addMonthsClamped(date, months) for "YYYY-MM-DD" strings: move to the target month and clamp the day to that month's last day.
questions.explain: Starting from day 1 of the target month avoids rollover; "day 0 of the next month" gives the target month's length.

questions.q: Write nextBusinessDay(date, holidays) that returns the next date after date that is not a Saturday, Sunday or in the holidays set. Dates are "YYYY-MM-DD" strings.
questions.explain: Keep stepping one calendar day at a time until the day is a weekday that is not a holiday. Holidays as date strings make the membership test a plain Set.has.

questions.q: Write isRealDate(text) that returns true only for "YYYY-MM-DD" strings naming a day that exists. Use a regular expression for the shape and a Date.UTC round trip for the day.
questions.explain: Date.UTC rolls impossible values over (30 February becomes 2 March, month 13 becomes January of the next year), so comparing the fields back catches them.

questions.q: Format the calendar date "2026-03-06" for a Nigerian customer as "Friday, 6 March 2026", in a way that shows the same day on any machine.
questions.explain: Midnight UTC formatted in UTC always shows the stored day. The en-NG locale puts the day before the month.

questions.q: Write isOpen(instant) for a Lagos shop open Monday to Saturday from 08:00 (inclusive) to 20:00 (exclusive) Lagos time. Use formatToParts with timeZone: "Africa/Lagos", hourCycle: "h23", weekday: "short" and hour: "numeric" in the "en-US" locale.
questions.explain: 07:00Z is 08:00 in Lagos (open); 19:00Z on Saturday is 20:00 (closed); Sunday is always closed. The boundaries are exactly where tests should look.
